nameStory: The By-the-wind Sailor gets its whimsical name from its most distinctive feature - a small, stiff triangular sail that catches ocean breezes and propels it across the water's surface. Like a tiny sailboat with no sailor aboard, it drifts wherever the wind takes it, earning it the alternative names 'sea raft' and 'little sail.'
description: The By-the-wind Sailor is a small, floating marine colony that looks like a translucent blue jellyfish with a built-in sail. Each individual is actually a colony of tiny animals working together, typically measuring less than 3 inches long. They're usually deep blue in color and spend their lives drifting on the ocean's surface, but strong winds can wash thousands of them onto New England beaches at once.

idTips.label: Triangular sail
idTips.description: Look for a clear, stiff triangular fin standing upright from the center - it feels firm and plastic-like when touched, unlike soft jellyfish tissue

idTips.label: Deep blue color
idTips.description: The body displays a rich, translucent blue color that's deeper and more vibrant than most jellyfish you'll encounter on beaches

idTips.label: Oval, flat body
idTips.description: The main body is oval-shaped and flattened like a small pancake, feeling somewhat rubbery but firmer than typical jellyfish

idTips.label: Hanging tentacles
idTips.description: Short, thread-like tentacles dangle from the underside - avoid touching these as they can cause mild skin irritation

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Most specimens are smaller than your palm, typically 1-3 inches long, making them much smaller than common jellyfish

idTips.label: Mass strandings
idTips.description: Often found in groups of hundreds or thousands washed up together after storms, carpeting stretches of beach in blue

habitat: By-the-wind Sailors live in the open ocean but occasionally wash ashore on New England's beaches, particularly sandy stretches along the coast from Maine to Connecticut. You're most likely to find them stranded on beaches after strong onshore winds or storms that blow them in from deeper waters.

seasonality.spring: Peak time for beach strandings as spring storms and changing wind patterns can blow large numbers onto shore from offshore waters.
seasonality.summer: Occasional strandings continue, especially after summer storms. Look for fresh specimens early morning after windy nights.
seasonality.fall: Another active period for beach wash-ups as autumn storms increase, though numbers are typically smaller than spring events.
seasonality.winter: Rarely encountered on beaches during winter months as they remain in warmer offshore waters.

funFact: By-the-wind Sailors are actually living sailing fleets - different populations have sails that are angled either to the left or right, causing them to sail in opposite directions and preventing the entire species from getting blown to the same place and starving!
confusionNotes: Most commonly mistaken for small blue jellyfish, but the upright triangular sail is a dead giveaway - no true jellyfish has this feature. Remember: if it has a sail sticking up, it's a By-the-wind Sailor, not a jellyfish.
contextualKnowledge: Despite looking like jellyfish, By-the-wind Sailors are actually more closely related to corals and sea anemones, belonging to the same group called cnidarians. Each 'individual' you find is really a colony of tiny polyps working together as a floating city.
compareHints: Velella velella is the only species in its genus worldwide, making it unique among ocean drifters. It's most similar to the Portuguese man o' war, but much smaller and with a triangular sail instead of an inflated balloon-like float. Unlike the man o' war's dangerous sting, By-the-wind Sailors cause only mild irritation to human skin.
